newsitem.title: NORWAY: Crown, election, economy weigh on Norway bonds.
newsitem.headline: Crown, election, economy weigh on Norway bonds.

text.p: 1400 GMT -- Norwegian long yields rose while short rates and the crown held relatively steady after Wednesday's fall.
The long end underperformed Germany while the yield spread with the 10-year Bund widened.

Dealers said uncertainty over the currency and September's election following a new opinion poll, together with reports of the central bank's concerns over credit growth, were pressing down on the market.
1400 GMT vs 1400 GMT on Wednesday
* 2007 bond yield four basis points higher at 6.09 pct
* Norway over Bunds gap four basis points wider at 41 points
* Three-month eurokrone unchanged at 4.04 pct
* Crown at 4.1470 against mark vs 4.1440
* Crown 102.28 vs inverse European Currency Unit index vs 102.14
Norwegian bond yields rose on Thursday on increasing nervousness ahead of parliamentary elections in September and fears of overheating in the economy, dealers said.
In the 10-year sector the yield spread with German Bunds widened four basis points to 41 points.

One analyst said the upward move could partly be linked to a delayed reaction to a sudden weakening of the crown a day-earlier, combined with the election's proximity and a report quoting the central bank expressing concern over sharp growth in lending.
Financial daily Dagens Naeringsliv carried the headline "Inflation bomb in the credit market", saying overall growth in lending had risen by 90 billion crowns in the last year.
"There was nothing new in this article but in a nervous market headlines can mean a lot," said one player.

Analyst Guttorm Egge at Fondspartner, however, said it was a favourable period to buy. Egge said he did not believe Norges Bank would raise official interest rates before the election and said he saw no reason for higher domestic rates relative to international levels, especially in the middle of the curve.

"Even though we have to go back to 1988 to find such high growth in the credit indicator as we are seeing now, there are big differences. People are now borrowing to buy residential property and not for consumption, like they did in the 80's" Egge said.
Another uncertainty in the market was a fresh opinion poll showing gathering support for the right-wing Progress Party.

The survey, carried out by Scanfact for daily Verdens Gang, gave Labour 29.5 percent, down 0.5 percent from June and down 7.4 percent from the 1993 election, with the Progress Party following second at 23.5 percent, a rise of seven percent from a similar poll in June and up 17.2 percent from the last election.
It was the third poll this month to show the Progress Party receiving more than 20 percent of voter support.

Parliament's three-party centrist bloc, seen as the main threat to Jagland's government, fell two percent from June to a total 23 percent, while the Conservatives slipped four percent to 14.5 percent from the June survey.
--Tanya Pang, Oslo newsroom +47 22 42 50 41
